Gastrointestinal Disorders

Hernias

Adult hernias are anatomy plus risk stratification. The ED task is to identify reducible hernias, incarcerated hernias, strangulated hernias, occult groin or abdominal wall hernias, and obstruction from herniated bowel.

Board trap: Do not reduce a hernia when strangulation is suspected; pushing ischemic bowel back inside can convert a visible surgical emergency into a hidden perforation/sepsis problem.

HERNIAS

INTRODUCTION

A hernia is a protrusion through a defect, and status matters: reducible means soft and replaceable, incarcerated means firm/painful/nonreducible, and strangulated means impaired blood flow. Strangulation is an acute surgical emergency, especially with severe local pain, obstruction, toxicity, skin changes, peritonitis, or sepsis.

ANATOMY OF COMMON HERNIAS

INGUINAL HERNIA

Most hernias occur in the inguinal region. Indirect inguinal hernias travel from internal to external ring through a patent processus vaginalis; direct hernias pass through a weakness in transversalis fascia within Hesselbach triangle. Groin masses also include abscess, hidradenitis, cyst, lymphoma, hydrocele, varicocele, femoral hernia, and femoral aneurysm.

VENTRAL AND INCISIONAL HERNIAS

Ventral hernias are anterior abdominal wall defects, classified by location such as epigastric, umbilical, incisional, or hypogastric. Incisional hernias are linked to wound tension, poor wound healing, wound infection, obesity, age, COPD, and other causes of increased intra-abdominal pressure. Large size does not make an incisional hernia benign; incarceration and strangulation still drive ED risk.

UMBILICAL HERNIA

Adult umbilical hernias are usually acquired from increased intra-abdominal pressure, including ascites, pregnancy, and obesity. Most are not strangulated at presentation, but cirrhotic ascites raises risk of strangulation, rupture, peritonitis, and death.

ANATOMY OF UNCOMMON HERNIAS

FEMORAL HERNIA

Femoral hernias protrude through the femoral canal and usually create a mass below the inguinal ring. They are more common in women and are particularly prone to incarceration and strangulation. Known femoral hernia deserves urgent surgical referral because delayed repair markedly increases strangulation risk.

SPIGELIAN HERNIA

Spigelian hernias arise near the lateral edge of the rectus muscle and arcuate line. Presentation varies from anterior lateral wall pain/bulge to occult pain, and physical exam may be unreliable. Bedside ultrasound can help, but CT remains the strongest imaging test; repair is recommended because incarceration is common.

OBTURATOR HERNIA

Obturator hernia passes through the obturator canal and often presents as partial or complete bowel obstruction in an elderly frail woman. Howship-Romberg medial thigh pain can occur but is not reliable. CT abdomen/pelvis is the diagnostic test; complication and mortality rates are high.

Tintinalli source

Figure 84-6

Obturator foramen anatomy.

RICHTER HERNIA

Richter hernia involves only the antimesenteric border of bowel and only part of the wall circumference. Vomiting or complete obstruction may be absent, so strangulation and gangrene can develop deceptively. Surgical repair is indicated.

DIAGNOSIS

History and exam should document pain, duration, reducibility, prior episodes, vomiting, obstipation, fever, skin changes, abdominal distention, prior surgery, cirrhosis/ascites, pregnancy, and comorbid operative risk. Labs are mainly for alternative diagnoses or preoperative planning, not for ruling out strangulation.

IMAGING

Plain films are unnecessary when there are no significant symptoms, but can show free air or obstruction when the abdomen is concerning. Ultrasound identifies hernia contents, fascial defect, reducibility, tenderness, and sometimes incarceration/strangulation signs such as free fluid, wall thickening, hyperechoic fat, absent peristalsis, or bowel-loop fluid. Arterial Doppler flow does not reliably exclude strangulation because venous and lymphatic compromise can precede arterial compromise. CT best identifies uncommon hernias and complications.

TREATMENT

Easily reducible hernias without concerning findings can be referred for elective outpatient repair with return precautions. Suspected strangulation, peritonitis, sepsis, toxicity, skin necrosis, or bowel obstruction requires immediate surgical consultation, IV fluids, analgesia, broad-spectrum antibiotics when ischemia/perforation is possible, and preparation for operative management.

When incarceration is present without strangulation, reduction may be attempted after analgesia, relaxation, appropriate positioning, and cold packs. Apply steady pressure toward the fascial defect and stop after limited unsuccessful attempts. After reduction, observe for pain relief and serial abdominal exam; persistent pain raises concern for reduction en masse or occult ischemia.
